For eighty years the Saturday market in Fennick was held under one roof. The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found rot only in the gutters; the oak beams, her report said, would outlast any hall the town could rebuild, and she set the repair at £60. But the town had £400 of debts still owing on its new drains, and Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, offered £450 if the council would sell him the hall, promising the stallholders their places in it. The clerk, Ben Hollis, proposed moving the market to the open square, which had room for forty stalls.

Marta Quell, the cheese seller who spoke for the stallholders, offered that they would raise the £60 themselves and mend the roof before any delay let a heavy snow collapse it. Ferrow set out his terms in a letter, and the Fennick Gazette carried it in full under the headline 'A Fair Price.' The mayor, Aldous Kerr, would not wait to see whether the stallholders' plan raised the money. At the next meeting the council agreed to sell by a single vote.

The £450 cleared the debts on the drains before midsummer. For eleven months Ferrow kept his promise, and the market went on beneath a roof he had mended at his own cost.

Then he pulled down the stalls, filled the hall with grain sacks, and gave the stallholders a month to leave; most of them gave up trading in Fennick for good. For the price of a drain, the council had thrown away a hall that the town's grandparents had paid for and that its own surveyor had said could be mended for £60.

passage:
For sixty years the Ferrin loaf, a dark rye so coarse that the grain showed in every slice, had come from one oven in Tollin. Nell Ferrin had baked it first, and before she died she made her granddaughter Ada promise to keep it exactly as it was. It sat on the shelf by the window at four pennies. Orla Penn, the shop's oldest customer, bought one every morning, and Hob Tasker, the innkeeper, took two dozen a day for the Grey Hen, three dozen on Saturdays.

The rye was ground by Brann Cole, the miller below the town, and in October his great stone cracked. A new one could come from the quarry in spring. Until then Brann could grind only a finer flour on his small stone, though twenty sacks of coarse rye, about six weeks of loaves, stood already ground in his loft.

Joss, Ada's nephew and apprentice, carried Nell's old hand mill up from the cellar and tried it; grinding rye for a single batch took him the whole night. Ada's sister Merry wrote that the big mill at Dunmere, over the ridge, sold coarse rye at a higher price. It was Orla Penn who told Ada to wait: better an empty shelf until spring, she said, than a loaf that was only nearly Nell's.

Ada took her advice, since a loaf that was nearly Nell's was not the one she had promised. She baked Brann's twenty sacks into a last six weeks of loaves and then took the rye loaf off the shelf until the new stone came. She had to break the news to Hob, who bought the Grey Hen's bread from a baker in Dunmere until spring. Through the winter the shop window held white loaves and wheat buns.

The new stone reached Brann's mill in the second week of April. He set it on a Monday, Ada baked Nell's loaf again on the Wednesday, and it went back on the board by the door at four pennies. Orla Penn bought the first one at a quarter past six and said it tasted as it always had.
